name: First Great Awakening
info: The First Great Awakening, also called the Evangelical Revival, was a series of Protestant revivals in Britain and its thirteen North American colonies in the 1730s and 1740s that stressed a personal new birth and renewed piety.

facts.where: Britain (England, Wales and Scotland), the thirteen North American colonies, and Pietist communities in continental Europe such as Herrnhut
facts.period: revivals in the colonies from the 1710s and 1720s; Northampton revival 1734–1735; Welsh revival from 1735; Whitefield's and Wesley's open-air preaching from 1739; a great and general Awakening in New England 1740–1743; waning by 1745; revivals in the southern backcountry and slave communities in the 1750s and 1760s
facts.figures: George Whitefield, itinerant preacher; John and Charles Wesley, founders of Methodism; Jonathan Edwards, Congregational minister at Northampton; Gilbert Tennent, Presbyterian New Side leader; James Davenport, controversial itinerant; Nicolaus Zinzendorf, Moravian patron; Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland in Wales; Samuel Davies, preacher to enslaved people
facts.outcome: Protestant churches split into supporters and opponents of revival; Methodist and Baptist churches grew, Congregational and Presbyterian churches divided in the colonies, and a common evangelical identity emerged; historians dispute how great its effects were

t: Revivalists taught that conversion was not only assent to correct doctrine but a new birth experienced in the heart, and that assurance of salvation was a normal expectation of the Christian life.
The revivals divided churches into pro-revival New Lights and anti-revival Old Lights, causing 98 schisms among New England Congregationalists, while Baptist and Methodist churches grew.
The historian Jon Butler has argued that the term Great Awakening is vague and exaggerated, because the revivals were regional and their effects minimal, while others see a larger impact.
dyk: In 1743 James Davenport ordered his followers at New London to burn wigs, cloaks, rings and other vanities, and also books by religious authors such as John Flavel and Increase Mather; he later published a retraction.
ev: Jonathan Edwards preaches on justification by faith alone, starting the Northampton revival, which spreads to 25 communities
John Wesley feels his heart strangely warmed at a Moravian meeting on Aldersgate Street
Refused pulpits in Bath and Bristol, George Whitefield begins open-air preaching at Kingswood and soon draws crowds of 10,000
Whitefield tours New England and preaches in Boston to about 15,000 and later to 30,000 people
The Presbyterian Synod of Philadelphia expels the New Side, which forms the Synod of New York
James Davenport orders the burning of wigs, cloaks, rings and books at New London
New Side Presbyterians found what becomes Princeton University
The Old Side and New Side Presbyterians reunite

sections.background:
Pietism, which emphasised heartfelt faith in reaction to what many saw as a spiritually dry Protestant scholasticism, prepared Europe for revival. Nicolaus Zinzendorf, a Saxon noble who had studied under the Pietist leader August Hermann Francke, invited members of the Moravian Church to his estates in 1722, where they founded a community at Herrnhut; it became a refuge for other Protestants as well, and Moravian societies were later established in England.

In the early 18th century the Thirteen Colonies were religiously diverse. Congregational churches were the established religion in New England, the Middle Colonies were religiously tolerant, and the Anglican Church was officially established in the South. Church membership was low because it had not kept up with population growth, and Enlightenment rationalism was leading many people towards atheism, Deism, Unitarianism and Universalism. The churches of New England had fallen into a "staid and routine formalism".

Ministers influenced by New England Puritanism, Scots-Irish Presbyterianism and European Pietism began calling for a revival of religion. Revivals became more frequent among New England Congregationalists in the 1710s and 1720s, but stayed local until an earthquake off Massachusetts in 1727 produced the first revival to receive widespread publicity.
sections.aims:
Revivalists built on Reformation Protestantism and added an emphasis on providential outpourings of the Holy Spirit. They taught that conversion was a "new birth" experienced in the heart, not only intellectual assent to correct doctrine, and that receiving assurance of salvation was a normal expectation. Extemporaneous preaching was meant to give listeners a deep personal conviction of their need for salvation through Jesus Christ.

The major figures, including Whitefield, Edwards, Gilbert Tennent, Jonathan Dickinson and Samuel Davies, were moderate evangelicals who preached a pietistic Calvinism shaped by the Puritan tradition. Their theology had three stages: conviction of sin, conversion, and consolation, the search for assurance, which could take months or even years. Edwards's sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" is given as an example of preaching meant to spark conviction.

The revivalists remained Calvinists, affirming original sin and unconditional election, yet they preached to everyone in their audiences. Some Calvinists thought it inappropriate to tell strangers that they could repent and be saved. Revivalists also distinguished true conversion, motivated by love of God and hatred of sin, from false conversion, motivated by fear of hell. John Wesley's Methodists named three foundations of faith: people are "dead in sin" by nature, they are "justified by faith alone", and faith produces inward and outward holiness.
sections.events:
The Evangelical Revival first broke out in Wales, where Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland were converted in 1735 and began preaching to large crowds in South Wales. In the colonies the most influential early revival was at Northampton, Massachusetts, in 1734–1735, led by Jonathan Edwards; it spread to 25 communities in western Massachusetts and central Connecticut and waned from 1737. In England Whitefield, refused pulpits in Bath and Bristol in February 1739, began field preaching at Kingswood and within a week drew crowds of 10,000; by May he was preaching to London crowds of 50,000. He left his Bristol followers with John Wesley, who preached to about 3,000 near Bristol on 2 April 1739.

Whitefield returned to the colonies in November 1739, preached in Philadelphia, and in 1740 toured New England, where on 12 October he preached to 30,000 people in Boston. Gilbert Tennent followed with a three-month preaching tour. In the summer of 1741 James Davenport arrived; his attacks on "unconverted" ministers led to his arrest in Connecticut, a finding of mental illness, and deportation, and he was again declared insane and expelled from Boston.

New England experienced a "great and general Awakening" between 1740 and 1743, with widespread emotional preaching and reactions such as fainting and weeping. By 1745 it had begun to wane, though revivals spread to the southern backcountry and to slave communities in the 1750s and 1760s.
sections.people:
In England the leaders were three Anglican priests, the brothers John and Charles Wesley and George Whitefield, who had belonged to the Holy Club at Oxford and had been called "Methodists" for their methodical piety. Whitefield became a celebrity through dramatic preaching and newspaper advertisements. John Wesley, after a failed mission to Georgia and encounters with Moravians, felt at Aldersgate Street in May 1738 that, in his words, "I felt my heart strangely warmed". His organisational skills, notably the societies and classes into which he gathered converts, made him the primary founder of Methodism.

In the colonies, William Tennent, Sr. trained nearly 20 Presbyterian revivalists at his Log College, among them his three sons and Samuel Blair. Theodorus Jacobus Frelinghuysen, a Dutch Reformed pietist, was called by Sydney Ahlstrom "an important herald, if not the father of the Great Awakening". Jonathan Edwards held to traditional Calvinism at a time when Arminian theology was popular among some clergy, and his A Faithful Narrative, published in England, made him a celebrity there.

Women were rarely allowed to preach or lead, but the revivals encouraged them to examine their feelings and write about them; Hannah Heaton, Phillis Wheatley and Sarah Osborn are among the writers named. Samuel Davies, later president of Princeton University, preached to enslaved people in unusually large numbers in Virginia.
sections.outcomes:
The revivals united evangelicals across denominations around shared beliefs, and also divided existing churches. Opponents accused the revivals of fostering disorder and fanaticism by letting the uneducated become itinerant preachers. In the colonies the Awakening split supporters, called New Lights, from opponents, called Old Lights. New England Congregationalists experienced 98 schisms, and around 100 Separatist congregations were organised, which were persecuted and in Connecticut denied the legal toleration given to Baptists, Quakers and Anglicans. Among Presbyterians the Old Side expelled the New Side in 1741; the split was healed by 1758.

Baptists benefited the most: by 1804 there were over 300 Baptist churches in New England, many gained from former New Light Congregationalists. Between 20,000 and 50,000 new members were admitted to New England's Congregational churches. By John Wesley's death in 1791 there were an estimated 71,668 Methodists in England and 43,265 in America.

The revival also reached Africans. The message of spiritual equality appealed to many enslaved people, and black people accepted Christianity in large numbers for the first time. Whitefield criticised cruel slaveholders but did not intend to abolish slavery; he lobbied to have slavery reinstated in Georgia and became a slaveholder himself. The first black Baptist churches were founded in Virginia, South Carolina and Georgia before the American Revolution.
sections.legacy:
Historian John Howard Smith noted that the Awakening made sectarianism an essential characteristic of American Christianity, even as it unleashed a strong impulse towards cooperation across denominations. Evangelicals regarded the new birth as a bond that transcended disagreements on doctrine and church order. In England Evangelical Anglicans grew into an important constituency within the Church of England, and Methodism developed from the ministries of Whitefield and Wesley. The revival also inspired new missionary societies, such as the Baptist Missionary Society in 1792.

It inspired evangelical educational institutions. New Side Presbyterians founded what would become Princeton University in 1746, and the efforts of Eleazar Wheelock led to what would become Dartmouth College in 1754, originally to train Native American boys for missionary work among their own people. Yale, at first resistant, came to embrace revivalism. The Awakening had little immediate effect on most Lutherans, Quakers and non-Protestants, but later gave rise to a schism among Quakers that persists to this day.

Its scale is disputed. Jon Butler has argued that historians should abandon the term Great Awakening, because the revivals were regional events in only half the colonies with minimal effects. Historians have also debated whether the Awakening influenced the American Revolution: Alan Heimert sees a major impact, but most historians think it had only a minor one.

summary: The First Great Awakening was a series of Protestant revivals in Britain and its thirteen North American colonies in the 1730s and 1740s, led by figures such as Whitefield, John Wesley and Edwards. It stressed the new birth, divided churches into New and Old Lights, and fostered a common evangelical identity.
references: Thomas S. Kidd, The Great Awakening: The Roots of Evangelical Christianity in Colonial America (Yale University Press, 2007)
Mark A. Noll, The Rise of Evangelicalism: The Age of Edwards, Whitefield and the Wesleys (Inter-Varsity, 2004)
John Howard Smith, The First Great Awakening: Redefining Religion in British America, 1725–1775 (Fairleigh Dickinson University Press, 2015)
Harry Stout, The Divine Dramatist: George Whitefield and the Rise of Modern Evangelicalism (William B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 1991)
W. R. Ward, The Protestant Evangelical Awakening (Cambridge University Press, 2002)
notes: Dates: start 1730 and end 1749 are approximations from the lede (1730s and 1740s); the article also says New England revival waned by 1745 and revivals continued in the southern backcountry and slave communities in the 1750s and 1760s. The first colonial revivals are placed in the 1710s and 1720s.
The article gives Whitefield's Bristol crowds as 10,000 within a week and London crowds of 50,000 by May 1739; kept as given.
The 1758 event (Old Side and New Side reunite) is dated by the article as 'By 1758', so the label is a year only as a latest date.
Davenport's burning of books and vanities is dated March 1743 at New London in the article; the year is used in the event list.

Left out: the Scottish revival (Cambuslang Work of 1742 is only named in passing) and Continental details beyond Herrnhut, for length. The article's Wales origin (1735) sits beside Northampton 1734; both are given as the article states.
